tldr: Philippart shows how Dev Containers let Docker be the only thing installed on a laptop, building a Java toolchain up from a devcontainer.json to shared features, templates and prebuilt images.
summary: Stéphane Philippart starts from familiar pain: reinstalling tools on a new machine, onboarding onto a project, giving up on an open source fix because of the setup, or wanting to try an AI assistant without letting it run rm -rf on your laptop. His answer is Dev Containers: local VS Code connects to a VS Code server inside a container, with the source mounted as a volume. In a live demo on a Mac with no Java installed, he adds a configuration from the Java template (Java 25 on Debian Trixie), reopens in the container and runs Java there. He then switches to a generic base image and uses features to install Java 26 from Temurin, Maven and JBang via SDKMAN, with customizations that pre-install the JBang and Red Hat Java extensions.

Each following step adds one more level of reuse. postCreateCommand runs a script, here installing the OVHcloud CLI and a JBang-installed httpd command, remoteEnv sets the PATH, and port forwarding opens the app in the host browser. He turns the script into a local feature (a folder with devcontainer-feature.json and install.sh), then into a remote feature published to the GitHub registry using Microsoft's feature starter repo and its GitHub Action. He also covers custom Dockerfiles pushed to a private registry, Docker Compose with a PostgreSQL service, custom templates from the template starter repo, and `devcontainer build --push`, which bakes everything into an image so the config shrinks to two lines. The downsides he lists: heavy images, rebuilds that need a network connection, and weak IntelliJ support (Ultimate only, plugins installed locally).
keyPoints: Features install tools such as Java 26 (Temurin), Maven and JBang into a generic image without writing a Dockerfile.
postCreateCommand covers tools that have no feature, and remoteEnv sets container environment variables such as PATH.

Local features live in .devcontainer/<name>/ with devcontainer-feature.json (options) and install.sh. The official feature-starter repo plus a GitHub Action publishes them to the GitHub registry so other projects can share them.
Templates (devcontainer-template.json with options) and the devcontainer CLI's build command can bake the whole setup into one image, so a project's config is just a name and an image.

Downsides: images can be heavy, every config change triggers a rebuild that needs internet, and the IntelliJ integration needs Ultimate and installs plugins locally, which Philippart says goes against the spirit of Dev Containers.
takeaways: Add a .devcontainer/devcontainer.json to one project, starting from an official template, and see whether new contributors need anything besides Docker.
Move repeated postCreateCommand scripts into a feature published from the devcontainers feature-starter repo, so a change only has to be made once.
Use Docker Compose in devcontainer.json to bring up the database next to the dev container instead of installing it locally.

quotes.text: If I succeed to create my Dockerfile, I think you can too.

watchIf: You onboard people onto projects with long setup instructions, or want a disposable, reproducible Java environment, and haven't used Dev Containers beyond the basics.
